props.title: True Confessions
props.initialSlug: Priests & murder collide in 1940s LA noir

sections.content: True Confessions stands as a masterful neo-noir that pairs Robert De Niro and Robert Duvall as brothers entangled in corruption and murder in 1940s Los Angeles. Drawing inspiration from the real-life Black Dahlia case, the film creates a haunting meditation on faith, power, and moral compromise. Like Chinatown (1974), it peels back LA's glossy veneer to expose institutional rot, but adds a spiritual dimension through De Niro's conflicted Catholic monsignor. The film's methodical pacing and muted tone echo The Friends of Eddie Coyle (1973), prioritizing character study over conventional thriller beats. Confidential|1997|Interwoven tale of police corruption in 1950s Hollywood|HBO Max The Black Dahlia|2006|Brian De Palma's stylized take on the infamous LA murder case|Prime

Director Ulu Grosbard brings a documentarian's eye to period Los Angeles, creating a world that feels lived-in rather than merely recreated. The approach shares DNA with Prince of the City (1981) and The Pope of Greenwich Village (1984) - other character-driven crime films more interested in moral ambiguity than clear-cut heroes and villains. The relationship between the brothers - one a priest, one a detective - provides the film's beating heart, examining how different paths toward justice can lead to devastating compromises. SUBHEAD: Religious Noir and Moral Ambiguity

True Confessions helped establish a vital sub-genre of noir focusing on religious themes and Catholic guilt, paving the way for films like The Name of the Rose (1986) and Calvary (2014). The film's exploration of institutional corruption within both the church and police force feels especially prescient today. Like Bad Lieutenant (1992), it presents faith not as an answer but as another complicated layer in characters' moral struggles.
